content: The publication titled Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing (July 2021) provides evidence from multiple countries on the usability and acceptability of self-testing for hepatitis C virus (HCV). The study was conducted by a team of experts, including Elena Ivanova Reipold, Thi Thuy Van Nguyen, Gamal Shihah, Ketevan Stvilia, Aliza Monroe-Wise, Cheng Wang, Muhammad S. Jamil, Cheryl C. Johnson, and Philippa Easterbrook, under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO). The findings are part of WHO's broader efforts to promote transparency and provide evidence-based guidance for HCV elimination strategies. Globally, less than 20% of individuals with HCV infection have been tested, and only about 25% of those diagnosed have received treatment. HCV self-testing (HCVST) is proposed as an additional strategy to expand access to testing and support global elimination efforts. The study assessed the usability and acceptability of HCVST among both general populations and key populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM) and people who inject drugs (PWID). The research involved observational studies conducted in five countries: Egypt (general population), China (MSM), Kenya (PWID), and Vietnam and Georgia (both MSM and PWID). The OraQuick® HCV Rapid Antibody Test, adapted for self-testing, was used as the prototype. Participants were provided with written and pictorial instructions for use (IFU) and conducted the self-test in a private setting under the observation of a trained professional. In Egypt, participants also received one-on-one demonstrations on how to use the test. Usability was evaluated by observing errors and difficulties during the self-testing process, while acceptability was assessed through semi-structured questionnaires. Participants interpreted their test results, which were then verified by observers. All participants were subsequently re-tested using a professional OraQuick® HCV test performed by trained providers. A total of 775 participants were enrolled across the five studies. The highest rates of participants completing all testing steps without errors were observed in Egypt and Georgia (>70%), while the lowest rates were among PWID in Kenya (30%) and Vietnam (46%). The most common error was incorrect sample collection. Agreement between participants and observers in interpreting test results ranged from 86% to 99%, and agreement between different operators ranged from 85% to 99%. Many PWID in Vietnam and Kenya required assistance to perform the self-test. The proportion of participants who found the test kit easy or very easy to use ranged from 55% in Egypt and 66% in Kenya to over 80% in other countries. Acceptability was high, with more than 90% of participants in four countries expressing willingness to use HCVST again and recommending it to family and friends. These studies are the first to demonstrate high usability and acceptability of HCVST globally, both in general and key populations. While most users were able to self-test with ease, assisted self-testing models may be necessary for certain populations, such as PWID. HCVST represents a promising tool for increasing testing coverage and achieving HCV elimination goals. The findings underscore the importance of considering HCVST as part of comprehensive strategies to address the global burden of hepatitis C.
